content: Studies on insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) that incorporate new products, such as pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs, are conducted to evaluate their survival and integrity under field conditions. These studies provide critical data on the lifespan of the product and help estimate the duration of its additional impact against malaria. A systematic review reported that two years after deployment, 34% of pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs were torn (defined as having a hole area ≥ 790 cm², rendering them unfit for use), compared to 28% of pyrethroid-only long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) and 43% of pyrethroid-PBO ITNs. This highlights differences in durability among the various ITN types. The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends deploying pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs instead of pyrethroid-only LLINs for malaria prevention in areas with pyrethroid resistance. This recommendation is based on moderate-certainty evidence that these ITNs are more effective in such settings. However, the recommendation to use pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs instead of pyrethroid-PBO ITNs is conditional, as the evidence is derived from only one trial conducted in Africa. The pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs combine two active ingredients: a pyrethroid and a pyrrole insecticide. Pyrethroids target the nervous system of mosquitoes, causing paralysis and rapid death, while chlorfenapyr disrupts mitochondrial ATP production, leading to energy depletion and cell dysfunction. This dual mechanism reduces the likelihood of cross-resistance to standard neurotoxic insecticides like pyrethroids. However, chlorfenapyr’s mode of action results in a slower kill (24–48 hours post-exposure) compared to pyrethroids. The systematic review included two trials from Africa, which evaluated the impact of pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs on malaria incidence and infection prevalence. In areas with high malaria transmission and pyrethroid-resistant mosquitoes, these ITNs reduced clinical malaria incidence by approximately 55% one year after deployment and by 40% two years post-deployment. Malaria infection prevalence was reduced by 20% after one year and by 45% after two years. Compared to pyrethroid-PBO ITNs, pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs showed little to no effect on clinical malaria incidence after one year but reduced it by 35% after two years. The trials also assessed ITN integrity. In Tanzania, 28% of pyrethroid-only LLINs, 34% of pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs, and 43% of pyrethroid-PBO ITNs were found to be torn after two years. The durability of ITNs is a critical factor in their effectiveness over time. The cost-effectiveness of pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs was evaluated in Tanzania. These ITNs were estimated to avert 152 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) per 10,000 population over two years, compared to 37 DALYs averted by pyrethroid-PBO ITNs. From a societal perspective, pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs were less costly and more effective than both pyrethroid-only LLINs and pyrethroid-PBO ITNs. Despite their benefits, the higher cost of pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs raises concerns about maintaining ITN coverage in resource-limited settings. National programs are encouraged to monitor insecticide resistance and consider cost implications when deploying these ITNs. WHO emphasizes the importance of ensuring equitable access to effective malaria prevention tools, particularly in areas with high malaria transmission and pyrethroid resistance. In conclusion, pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs represent a promising tool for malaria control in areas with pyrethroid-resistant vectors. However, their deployment should be guided by local vector resistance profiles, cost considerations, and the need to maintain high ITN coverage. Further research is needed to evaluate their long-term impact, durability, and cost-effectiveness in diverse settings.
